summary: Defines how an OSPF router advertises the types of Maximum SID Depth it supports, at node or link level. Controllers can use this to know whether a given stack of segment identifiers can be handled.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8476 lets an OSPF router say how many labels it can push onto a packet. A controller that computes paths needs that number, because a path asking for more labels than a router can carry will fail. The router publishes one number for the whole device and, if it differs, one number for each link.

subtitle: How an OSPF router tells controllers how deep a stack of segment identifiers it can push onto a packet.

tldr.problem: When a controller computes a Segment Routing path, it must know how many segment identifiers each node on the path can handle, or the path it computes may be impossible to carry.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a Node MSD TLV to the OSPF Router Information LSA and a Link MSD sub-TLV to the link advertisements, each holding one or more pairs of an MSD type and a value between 0 and 255.
tldr.outcome: Every OSPF router in the network can publish its depth, and the controller can check a computed path against it before it is installed. A wrong value causes either a path that cannot be computed or a path that cannot be carried.

facts.label: Meaning of an MSD value of zero
facts.value: No stack of any depth can be imposed

today: RFC 8476 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It allocates the Node MSD TLV type 12 in the OSPF Router Information TLVs registry, and the link sub-TLV types 6 and 9 for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3. The IGP MSD-Types registry it points to is created in RFC 8491.

sections.title: Why the Depth Has to Be Known
sections.content:
When Segment Routing paths are computed by a centralised controller, it is critical that the controller learns the Maximum SID Depth that can be imposed at each node or link on a given path. This ensures that the SID stack depth of a computed path does not exceed the number of SIDs the node is capable of imposing.

PCEP defines how to signal MSD in the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol. But if PCEP is not supported or configured on the head-end of an SR tunnel or a Binding-SID anchor node, and the controller does not take part in IGP routing, it has no way of learning the MSD of nodes and links. BGP-LS, the distribution of link-state and traffic engineering information using BGP, defines a way to expose topology and associated attributes and capabilities of the nodes to a centralised controller, and MSD signalling by BGP-LS has been defined separately. Typically, BGP-LS is configured on a small number of nodes that do not necessarily act as head-ends. For BGP-LS to signal MSD for all the nodes and links in the network where MSD matters, MSD capabilities should be advertised by every OSPF router in the network.

Other kinds of MSD are known to be useful. One example is Entropy Readable Label Depth, which a head-end uses to insert an entropy label at a depth where it can be read by transit nodes. This document defines an extension to OSPF used to advertise one or more types of MSD at node and link granularity, and it is expected that new MSD types will later signal additional capabilities such as entropy labels, SIDs imposed through recirculation, or SIDs for another data plane such as IPv6.

MSD advertisements may be useful even if Segment Routing itself is not enabled: in a non-SR MPLS network, MSD defines the maximum label depth.
sections.plainLanguage: A controller that builds a path out of numbered instructions needs to know how many instructions each router can hold. Without that number it can produce a path that no router can carry, and the failure appears only later, in the data plane. OSPF already tells routers about the topology, so it is the natural place to publish the depth as well.

sections.title: Terms Used Here
sections.content:
The RFC uses the terms defined in RFC 7770, and adds some of its own.

  • MSD, Maximum SID Depth, is the number of SIDs supported by a node or by a link on a node.
  • SID is the Segment Identifier defined in RFC 8402.
  • Label imposition is the act of modifying or adding labels to the outgoing label stack associated with a packet. It includes replacing the label at the top of the label stack with a new label, and pushing one or more new labels onto the label stack.

The number of labels imposed is the sum of the number of labels replaced and the number of labels pushed. The RFC also names OSPF as Open Shortest Path First, LSA as Link State Advertisement, and RI as Router Information.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ideas matter. Maximum SID Depth is how many identifiers a router can carry. Label imposition is what a router does when it forwards a packet: it swaps the top label for another, pushes more labels on, or both. The depth limit counts both actions together.

sections.title: The Node MSD TLV
sections.content:
The Node MSD TLV sits in the body of the OSPF Router Information Opaque LSA and carries the provisioned SID depth of the router that originated the RI LSA. Node MSD is the smallest MSD supported by the node on the set of interfaces configured for use by the advertising IGP instance. The values may be learned through a hardware interface or may be provisioned by an operator.

The TLV has a type of 12. Its length is variable, a multiple of 2 octets, and represents the total length of the value field in octets. The value consists of one or more pairs, each a 1-octet MSD-Type followed by a 1-octet MSD-Value. The MSD-Type is one of the values defined in the IGP MSD-Types registry, and the MSD-Value is a number in the range 0 to 255. For all MSD types, 0 represents the lack of ability to impose a stack of any depth, and any other value represents the depth of the node; that value must represent the lowest value supported by any link configured for use by the advertising OSPF instance.

The TLV is optional and applies to both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3. The scope of the advertisement is specific to the deployment.

When several Node MSD TLVs arrive from one router, the receiver must use the first occurrence of the TLV in the Router Information LSA. If the TLV appears in several RI LSAs with different flooding scopes, the one in the area-scoped LSA must be used. If it appears in several RI LSAs with the same flooding scope, the one in the LSA with the numerically smallest Instance ID must be used and the others ignored. The RI LSA can be advertised at any of the defined opaque flooding scopes, which are link, area or Autonomous System, and area-scoped flooding is recommended for the Node MSD TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: The router publishes one number for itself, the depth it can manage across all of its interfaces. It sits in the Router Information LSA, which OSPF already floods. The value is a byte, so the range is 0 to 255, and zero means the router cannot carry a stack at all.

sections.title: The Link MSD Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The Link MSD sub-TLV carries the MSD of the interface associated with the link. The values may be learned through a hardware interface or provisioned.

For OSPFv2 the link-level MSD-Value is advertised as an optional sub-TLV of the OSPFv2 Extended Link TLV, with a type of 6. For OSPFv3 it is advertised as an optional sub-TLV of the E-Router-LSA TLV, with a type of 9.

The length is variable and the same as in the Node MSD TLV. The value again consists of one or more pairs of a 1-octet MSD-Type and a 1-octet MSD-Value, with the type taken from the IGP MSD-Types registry. The MSD-Value field holds the Link MSD of the router that originated the corresponding LSA, in the range 0 to 255. For all MSD types, 0 represents the lack of ability to impose a stack of any depth, and any other value represents the depth of that particular link when used as an outgoing interface.

If the sub-TLV is advertised several times for the same link in different OSPF Extended Link Opaque LSAs or E-Router-LSAs originated by the same router, the copy in the OSPFv2 Extended Link Opaque LSA with the smallest Opaque ID, or in the OSPFv3 E-Router-LSA with the smallest Link State ID, must be used by receiving routers. That situation should be logged as an error.
sections.plainLanguage: A link can have a different limit from the router as a whole, so the link advertisement carries its own value. The two protocol versions put it in different places, but the number means the same thing: how deep a stack that interface can push.

sections.title: Which Value to Use
sections.content:
When a Link MSD is present for a given MSD type, its value must take precedence over the Node MSD. When a Link MSD type is not signalled but the Node MSD type is, the Node MSD value must be used as the MSD value for that link.

In order to increase flooding efficiency, it is recommended that routers with homogeneous Link MSD values advertise just the Node MSD value, since a single advertisement then covers every link.

The meaning of the absence of both Node and Link MSD advertisements for a given MSD type is specific to that type. Generally, it can only be inferred that the advertising node does not support advertisement of that type. In some cases the lack of advertisement might instead imply that the functionality associated with the type is not supported, and the correct interpretation must be specified when an MSD type is defined.
sections.plainLanguage: Two rules settle any question. A link value wins over the router value, and if there is no link value, the router value applies. A router whose links all behave the same is asked to advertise only the one number, to save flooding effort.

sections.title: Registry Allocations
sections.content:
The specification updates several existing OSPF registries.

IANA allocated TLV type 12 from the OSPF Router Information TLVs registry defined in RFC 7770, for the Node MSD. IANA allocated sub-TLV type 6 from the OSPFv2 Extended Link TLV Sub-TLVs registry, for the OSPFv2 Link MSD, and sub-TLV type 9 from the OSPFv3 Extended-LSA Sub-TLVs registry, for the OSPFv3 Link MSD.
sections.plainLanguage: Three numbers are registered: 12 for the node level TLV inside the Router Information LSA, 6 for the link value in OSPFv2, and 9 for the link value in OSPFv3.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security concerns for OSPF are addressed in RFC 7474, RFC 4552 and RFC 7166, with further analysis in RFC 6863, and the security considerations of RFC 7770, RFC 7684 and RFC 8362 apply here as well.

Implementations must ensure that malformed TLVs and sub-TLVs defined in this document are detected and do not give an attacker a way to crash the OSPF router or routing process. Reception of malformed TLVs or sub-TLVs should be counted or logged for further analysis, and that logging should be rate limited so that a denial-of-service attack cannot overload the OSPF control plane.

Advertising an incorrect MSD value has negative consequences. If the value is smaller than what is supported, path computation may fail to compute a viable path. If it is larger than what is supported, an attempt may occur to instantiate a path that the head-end, the node performing the SID imposition, cannot support. The presence of this information may also inform an attacker of how to induce either of those conditions.

There is no denial-of-service risk specific to this extension, and it is not vulnerable to replay attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The depth a router advertises is information an attacker could use, so a wrong value has real consequences: too small and the controller cannot build a path at all, too large and it builds one the router cannot carry. Implementations must also handle malformed advertisements without crashing.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: TLV type, the value 12 for Node MSD.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total length of the value field in octets, a multiple of 2.

fields.desc: Which kind of depth is being advertised, from the IGP MSD-Types registry.

fields.name: MSD-Value
fields.desc: Depth from 0 to 255; 0 means the node cannot impose a stack of any depth.

How a receiver picks the value that applies to a link

items.title: Link value first
items.text: When a Link MSD is present for a type, its value takes precedence over the Node MSD.

items.title: Node value as fallback
items.text: When a link does not signal that type, the Node MSD value applies to that link.

items.title: One number is enough
items.text: Routers whose links all have the same value are asked to advertise only the Node MSD, which floods less.

items.title: Silence has a meaning
items.text: Missing advertisements usually mean the node cannot advertise that type; the exact meaning must be defined per type.
